data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"18 is the smallest positive solution, found by first solving the transformed system x \u2261 -2 (mod 5) and x \u2261 -3 (mod 7), where the residues are each one less than a common value of -1 relative to their moduli, and correcting.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the constant-difference shortcut somehow applies with offset -2 giving x \u2261 -2 (mod 35) \u2192 33 as the smallest positive solution, this candidate is overturned (but 18 < 33 and 18 satisfies both, so 33 is not smallest).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If a positive integer smaller than 18 satisfies both congruences, the offset analysis is incomplete.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Rewrite the remainders: x \u2261 3 (mod 5) means x + 2 \u2261 0 (mod 5), so x \u2261 -2 (mod 5). And x \u2261 4 (mod 7) means x + 3 \u2261 0 (mod 7), so x \u2261 -3 (mod 7). The offsets from the moduli are -2 and -3, which are NOT equal. The constant-difference shortcut (which would require both offsets to be the same value c, giving x \u2261 c mod lcm) does NOT apply directly here. Instead, the difference between the offsets is -2 - (-3) = 1, which must be absorbed by the modular structure. Testing the residue chain x = -2 + 5t: for t = 0, x = -2 \u2261 5 (mod 7); t = 1, x = 3 \u2261 3 (mod 7); t = 2, x = 8 \u2261 1; t = 3, x = 13 \u2261 6; t = 4, x = 18 \u2261 4 (mod 7).
